title: Flicker vs. Sheldon: The Great Race
markdown:
The Meadowbrook Pet Show smelled of hay, lemonade, and a little too much pride. Bunting snapped along the fence. Somewhere a goat was being brushed within an inch of its dignity. Benji, who spent ordinary Saturdays helping with the show telescope, had no interest in goats. He had Flicker.

Flicker was a hummingbird the colour of wet leaves after rain, with a throat like a chip of sky. He did not land so much as arrive. When Benji said he was the fastest thing in the field, Flicker proved it by being somewhere else.

“He leaves the wind itself panting,” Benji told Dapple.

Dapple did not pant. She stood with her tortoise, Sheldon, whose shell had the patient shine of a well-kept pebble. Sheldon was already facing the right way, which, Dapple felt, counted for something.

“Sheldon may be slow,” she said, “but he is persistent.”

“Steady is boring,” Benji scoffed. “You need zoom, not slow-motion.”

Ms. Quill heard them. She was the owl judge, spectacles on her beak, a pocket watch in her claw that had timed more arguments than races. She swooped onto the fence post with a rustle like turning pages.

“Hoo-hoo. Let numbers settle this. A race. Ten whisker-lengths to that dandelion. Flicker against Sheldon. Each carries a daisy. We time them thrice. The numbers reveal all.”

Benji beamed. “Flicker will win before Sheldon even wiggles a toe.”

Dapple only smiled. “We’ll do our best.”

The first race was a streak. Flicker took the daisy, became a green-and-blue smear, set it on the dandelion, and was back before Benji had finished drawing breath. Five seconds. Sheldon set off as if the grass had asked him politely. Plod. Plod. Plod. Daisy down. Amble home. Forty-five seconds.

“Eight times faster!” Benji waved both arms, which did not help Flicker, who was already preening.

“Patience,” said Ms. Quill. “More data.”

Second race: Flicker nine seconds, a little crosswind catching one wing. Sheldon forty-seven, the same drumbeat of feet. Third: Flicker six. Sheldon forty-six.

Ms. Quill scratched the times on a flat stone:

Flicker: 5, 9, 6
Sheldon: 45, 47, 46

Benji squinted. Flicker’s numbers jumped like grasshoppers. Sheldon’s sat together like pebbles in a pocket.

“Flicker’s smaller! He wins!”

Ms. Quill’s eyes twinkled, which on an owl is a serious business. “Look closer. Flicker’s times leap. His speed is astonishing, and it varies. Sheldon’s times stay near one another. You can count on them. A reliable drumbeat.”

Benji frowned at the stone. “Consistent. But Flicker is faster.”

“Indeed the swiftest,” Ms. Quill said. “Consistency is another virtue. Performance you can count on.”

She produced a ribbon the colour of a clear afternoon. “The Most Consistent Performer.” Sheldon accepted it with a slow, dignified blink, as if he had been expecting the ribbon to arrive eventually and saw no reason to rush the moment.

Benji looked from Flicker’s still-humming wings to Sheldon’s unhurried blink. Speed was one kind of winning. The stone had shown another.

“So Flicker is fastest,” he said, a smile arriving the long way round, “but Sheldon is most dependable?”

“Precisely.”

They did not need a speech about nature and numbers. The stone was still there in the grass, the three pairs of times sitting in two very different shapes. Benji crouched and tapped Flicker’s middle nine with a fingernail.

“What if we raced in wind?” he asked. “Would his numbers jump more?”

Ms. Quill wound her watch. “That,” she hooted, “would be another set of numbers. I shall be here. Bring daisies.”

Dapple offered Benji a lemonade. Sheldon wore the blue ribbon as if it weighed nothing, which, compared with being a tortoise, it did. Flicker, who had not been asked for his opinion on statistics, shot to the dandelion anyway, just to keep in practice.
characters: Benji (telescope helper), Dapple (friend), Ms. Quill (owl judge), Flicker (hummingbird), Sheldon (tortoise)
